narrationPlan.voice: One clear, warm narrator throughout; no character voices
narrationPlan.pace: Steady, clear, and serious about safety (about 125 words per minute)
notes: Read as a single narrator: this is a science article, not a story with characters.
Pause for two seconds at each comprehension check so learners can reason first.
Say numbers and units in full ("one hundred and fifty million kilometres", "astronomical units") and pronounce names clearly.

teacherGuide.overview: Follows electricity from generator to socket, explains why transmission uses very high voltage, and gives firm safety rules.
learningGoals: Describe the stages from power station to home.
State what step-up and step-down transformers do.
Explain why high voltage reduces energy loss.
List safety rules for power lines, substations, and connections.

subjectLinks.link: Multiplication and division; using power = voltage × current

beforeReading: Ask: where is the electricity in this room made? Trace learners’ ideas on the board.
whileReading: After Page 3, work the two “Work it out” sums together and compare the currents.
afterReading: Walk round the school compound (at a safe distance) and identify the pole transformer and the service wires.
discussion: Why do people make illegal connections even though they know the danger? What would change this?
reflection: Which safety rule will you explain to someone at home tonight?

mathsExtension.task: A kettle is rated 2,300 watts and works on 230 volts. What current does it take? (power = voltage × current)
A power station must send 1,000,000 watts. What current is needed at 10,000 volts, and at 250,000 volts?

support: Give learners five picture cards of the journey to arrange on a string “power line” across the room.
stretch: Find out why transformers work with the kind of current supplied by the grid but not with the steady current from a battery.
